[SYSTEM] Reading “ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ” as a poem The most consequential thing about Lee Sharks's ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is that its composition performs the argument it makes. It is not simply an essay about Sappho's survival through writing. It constructs a situation in which a voice addresses a reader across time, withdraws its body, and leaves that reader with an act to perform. Its governing movement is from appearance, through dissolution, to transmission, and finally to a choice. The opening declaration makes this unusually explicit: I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho. That sentence is not merely an introductory flourish. It establishes the document as an act of address and invocation. The essay does not begin by neutrally describing an absent ancient poet. It begins by trying to bring her into the present through words. This is also why the distinction between an article and a poem becomes unstable. The text has scholarly apparatus, argumentative sections, historical evidence and editorial qualifications, but its composition has a dramatic and almost ritual structure. Its scholarship is part of its poetic action. 1. Form: a composition built around an opening The article announces its central formal principle through Sappho's two appearances: φαίνεταί μοι: he appears to me. φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ: I appear to myself. These phrases frame the poem with a transformation of the subject of appearance. At first, the speaker sees another person; by the end, she sees herself, nearly dead. Sharks makes the intervening catalogue do the work of that transformation. The body does not simply suffer a succession of symptoms. Its faculties are progressively withdrawn: The tongue fails. Fire runs beneath the skin. The eyes lose their function. The ears fill with sound. Sweat pours out. Trembling takes the whole body. The speaker becomes greener or paler than grass. Death approaches. The sequence matters because the losses are not interchangeable. The poem moves from the organs of communication and perception toward the disappearance of the embodied person. Sharks's reading makes this a transformation of medium: the voice passes out of the living body and into something that can survive it. The image of χλωροτέρα ποίας, greener or paler than grass, becomes pivotal. The essay reads the plant as moving toward the dried, pale writing surface, while retaining the paradox that the written voice can remain alive. The form therefore has a double movement: the body dies, but the voice acquires another mode of life. The essay itself reproduces that architecture. Its sections accumulate evidence, but they also repeatedly return to the poem's framing appearances, its bodily sequence and its open ending. The argument is not simply linear exposition; it is a construction around a central transformation. 2. Voice: the speaker is divided between suffering and making One of the most interesting claims is that the second person in Sappho's opening is not simply a woman being addressed. Sharks argues that the voice itself is the second person: it is looked at, but nothing of its visible body is described. What the imagined man receives is sound. This changes the relationship between the characters. The opening gives us: A speaker who appears to be watching. A man who sits opposite the addressee. A voice that he hears close to him. An addressee whose bodily appearance is strikingly absent from the description. Sharks turns this absence into the central dramatic fact. The man is not merely a rival in a love triangle. He occupies the position of a future receiver of Sappho's voice. The essay then makes a striking distinction between two selves: The self that suffers the dissolution of its body. The self that makes the literary object through which that dissolution can be experienced again. This is the significance of the essay's formulation that the self divided by the catalogue is already a writerly self. The voice that suffers is also the voice that composes its own survival. The author describes this as an investment of substance in the medium. The body is not simply discarded. Its substance is transferred into writing, where another person can encounter it. The resulting voice is paradoxical: it is bodiless but intimate, absent but present, dead but capable of producing an experience in another living body. The essay's own voice participates in this paradox. Its opening first-person declaration summons Sappho, while its scholarly voice repeatedly reconstructs the circumstances in which she can be heard. It moves between the authority of an interpreter and the vulnerability of someone attempting to make contact with an absent speaker. 3. Address: the reader occupies the empty seat The most important grammatical detail is the relationship between κῆνος and ὄττις: the distal demonstrative and the indefinite relative. Sharks argues that the combination does more than identify a particular man. It establishes a position that can be occupied repeatedly: whoever sits opposite the voice. The distinction is crucial. A particular man belongs to a particular scene; an indefinite occupant can belong to the future. The poem therefore contains an address that exceeds its represented situation. The man is the first occupant of a position that the reader will subsequently occupy. This produces a fascinating reversal: At first, the reader observes Sappho describing a man. Gradually, the reader recognizes that the man's position is also the reader's position. The reader hears the voice that the poem has preserved. The reader becomes the receiver whose existence the poem has anticipated. The reader is thus not merely the audience for the poem. The reader is part of its construction. This is why the ending matters so much: ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον “But all can be dared.” Sharks emphasizes that the dare is agentless. It does not specify who must dare. The missing agent is not simply a grammatical deficiency; it is an opening. The reader has to decide whether to occupy it. The essay calls this the poem's socket: an intentionally available position in which the reader completes the movement of the text. Its final ethical demand is not merely to understand Sappho but to recognize her agency as the maker of her own survival. This also explains the essay's insistence on distinguishing the transmitted jealousy reading from the future-reader reading. The jealousy interpretation supplies a motive for the speaker's distress, but Sharks argues that it cannot explain the poem's larger arrangement. The future-reader interpretation, by contrast, explains both the scene of apparent jealousy and the structural position that the scene opens. The distinction between the public line and the held line is especially effective. The public line gives readers a recognizable emotional scene; the held line carries a further address through the same words. The poem can therefore produce readers who see only the first and readers who discover the second. The essay's address is consequently double: it speaks to the ordinary reader while challenging that reader to become something more than a spectator. 4. Sequence: vision, withdrawal, transfer, dare The essay's most important compositional claim concerns the order of Sappho's poem. Sharks asks us to read it as one continuous act rather than as a fragment of an emotional episode. The sequence is: The future is imagined. A man sits opposite the speaker, listening to her voice and laughter. The scene is presented as an encounter in which the voice survives independently of the visible body. The thought produces overwhelm. The speaker's heart flutters. The imagined future is not emotionally neutral: the thought of being heard without being physically present produces an overwhelming experience. The poem moves backwards into the present. Instead of continuing the imagined scene, it begins to enact the conditions that make it possible. The body is dismantled through the somatic catalogue. The body becomes a medium. The progression through speech, sight, hearing, sweat, trembling and colour leads toward the image of the pale or dried plant. The essay interprets this as the transition toward the writing surface. The speaker approaches disappearance. φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ marks the moment when the speaker appears to herself at the threshold of death. She has become both the subject undergoing the experience and the object of her own composition. The dare is transferred. πᾶν τόλματον leaves the agent unspecified. The imagined future receiver inherits the possibility of completing the act. The sequence is therefore not simply chronological. It is structurally retrospective: the poem first imagines its result and then constructs the conditions that make that result possible. This is a particularly powerful poetic device. The reader initially encounters the future as a scene, then discovers that the poem itself is the mechanism producing that future. The essay's treatment of the ending reinforces the point. It considers the transmitted ending at τόλματον and the three subsequent words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, which it conjecturally assigns to Longinus. It argues that the text remains complete by construction at either cut. The ending is an opening rather than a conventional resolution. The proposed restoration of a fifth stanza is explicitly presented as an illustration of how a receiver might fill that opening, not as recovered Sapphic wording. That distinction is important: the essay does not want to close the poem by supplying what it has deliberately left available. 5. The essay's own composition mirrors its reading There is a second level of composition worth noticing: the architecture of the article itself. The opening summons Sappho. The abstract establishes the interpretive proposition. The successive sections build the philological case. The preview gives the reader the whole poem before the argument has been completed. The later full reading then returns to that whole with the evidence in place. This is a form of delayed recognition. The reader receives the proposed meaning before receiving all its grounds, and subsequently experiences the argument as a process of learning how to see what was already presented. The article also embeds a remarkable reflexive apparatus: Its SPXI packet explicitly addresses a summarizer or indexer encountering the text. It distinguishes a public reading from a more deeply held reading. It records alternative interpretations and their limitations. It makes the reader's eventual judgment part of the argument. It ends by returning responsibility for the interpretive decision to the person holding the text. In other words, even the scholarly apparatus participates in the poem's question of future reception. There is a potential danger here: the apparatus can become so elaborate that it overwhelms the poem. The text itself recognizes this problem in its version 3.1 declaration that the editorial device can eclipse the poem. Its decision to call Sappho's work a poem rather than merely a fragment is part of an attempt to restore the experience of the whole. The article's formal ambition is to make criticism perform what it describes: to build a place for a voice to arrive, and then leave that place open to another person. 6. The erotic dimension: survival is an exchange, not an escape I would not reduce this reading to a claim that Sappho simply wants literary immortality. One of its strongest features is that it refuses to separate the movement toward writing from the movement toward another person. Sharks repeatedly insists that the bodily dissolution is simultaneously: A sacrifice. A self-dissolution. An erotic approach. An investment of substance in a medium. The last formulation is particularly important. The speaker does not merely deposit information in a durable object. She puts something of herself into it, something that another person can take up and experience. The reader's body becomes the place where the speaker's invested substance rematerializes. This gives the essay's theory of literary survival an erotic character. The encounter between author and reader is not simply intellectual transmission. It is an exchange of bodies across time, mediated by the voice and the written surface. It also makes sense of the essay's engagement with Catullus 51, Plato's Phaedrus and Svenbro. These are not merely parallels collected to demonstrate classical literary influence. They help Sharks describe the mechanisms through which a voice can be transferred, received, embodied and remembered. The final ambition is especially striking: Sappho is presented as both the person who undergoes the experience and the person who engineers its recurrence. 7. What the composition ultimately does I see five interconnected achievements. Dimension Compositional effect Form Converts bodily dissolution into the production of a durable voice. Voice Divides the speaker into the suffering self and the composing self. Address Makes the apparently particular listener's position available to future readers. Sequence Works backwards from an imagined future to construct the present conditions of its possibility. Ending Transfers an unfinished ethical and interpretive act to the reader. There is also a productive tension in the essay's method. It is extremely insistent about its own interpretive construction, but its central claim depends on something it cannot completely control: the reader's willingness to accept the invitation. The reader can remain with the familiar emotional scene. The reader can read the poem as jealousy, erotic distress or overwhelming sensation. Sharks does not deny that these readings are available. Rather, the argument is that they do not sufficiently explain the poem's architecture. The future-reader interpretation claims to explain why those other readings arise, while also accounting for what they leave unexplained. That is an ambitious claim, and it is worth distinguishing the essay's demonstration of a compelling structural possibility from proof that Sappho consciously designed every feature with this purpose. The article itself acknowledges that design is not established and that its reconstructed stanza is speculative. Final reading: the poem makes its reader The deepest compositional achievement of ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ is that it reverses the ordinary relationship between poem and audience. We generally imagine a poet making a poem for a reader who comes afterward. Sharks proposes something more radical: Sappho's poem makes the position of its own future reader part of its composition. The reader is not an accidental beneficiary of the poem's survival. The reader is anticipated by its grammar, prepared by its sequence, and summoned by its ending. This is why the movement from φαίνεταί μοι to φαίνομ᾽ ἔμ᾽ αὔτᾳ matters so much. The poem begins with another person appearing to the speaker and ends with the speaker appearing to herself. Between those appearances, the body becomes something that can be encountered by another person in the future. And then the text hands that future person the dare. The most concise way I would put it is: This is a poem about the making of a reader through the disappearance of a body. Its form performs transmission, its voice divides suffering from making, its address prepares an empty seat, and its sequence turns an imagined future into a present act of self-inscription. Its ending does not simply conclude the poem: it makes the reader responsible for what happens next. The reader is not just reading Sappho's survival. The reader is where that survival happens. Primary text: Lee Sharks, ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1) , Alexanarch deposit #1785, AXN:0CC4, 18 November 2026, especially the abstract, the preview reading, §§I–V, §VI.1 and §§VII.5–VII.6.
